# Tool-Connected Design Environments {#sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us."*
>
> — John Culkin, *Saturday Review* (1967) [@Culkin1967Schoolman]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** John Culkin, an American media scholar writing to explain
Marshall McLuhan's ideas, observed that tools reshape how people work. The line
is often credited to McLuhan, but it is Culkin's, a small provenance lesson of
its own. An architecture tool also shapes what a method can change and what an
architect can observe. Those limits must be explicit when the method acts
through the tool.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
What must surround real architecture tools so an AI-assisted method can use
them safely, reproducibly, and within declared limits?
:::

A tool command is not an environment. An architect can launch a simulator,
compiler, formal engine, or physical-design flow and still be unable to say
which candidate ran, which state the tool inherited, what an unfamiliar
warning meant, or whether a retry repeated the same work. AI-assisted methods
make this gap harder to ignore because they can issue requests faster than a
person can inspect the state around every invocation.

Consider a scoped cache study. It compares a rerun 2\ MB L2 baseline with
3\ MB and 4\ MB alternatives, and only `l2.capacity` may change. One SRAM
evaluation per capacity precedes at most four cycle-level attempts. The
requested returns include area, access time, cache-local energy and leakage,
matched frame data, capacity misses, and subsystem dynamic plus leakage power.
The example is called `XR-L2-CAP-A`. It is detailed enough to expose the
environment problem without requiring a particular method or orchestration
strategy.

The request is precise enough to select tools, but it is not executable yet.
Each represented candidate must become the exact configuration each tool
expects. Workload, software, libraries, process assumptions, and tool versions
must travel with it. Long jobs enter queues and may wait for licenses. A tool
may crash, time out, finish with a missing report, or exit successfully after
running the wrong top-level design. Returned files may arrive hours later and
out of order.

The environment handles those mechanics. It establishes that requested work
reached a named tool against a named state and records what the attempt
produced. It does not establish that the resulting number is a valid
measurement or that the candidate is good. This distinction separates a
well-formed run from a supported architecture claim. Interpreting the return
and judging the claim require additional checks beyond the environment.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Distinguish a tool, simulator, wrapper, harness, and complete environment.
- Specify environment state, legal actions, observations, transitions, costs,
  stopping conditions, and failure behavior.
- Establish a pinned starting state and control or report nondeterministic tool
  behavior.
- Design typed interfaces that preserve parameters, units, permissions,
  errors, raw output, and tool-specific meaning.
- Coordinate asynchronous and dependent runs within authority, security, time,
  compute, model, tool, and license limits.
- Recover from failed work without confusing process failure with a measured
  design violation or reusing stale state.
- Report enough identity, status, artifacts, warnings, versions, and cost to
  support replay, repeatability analysis, and independent reproduction.
- Carry one candidate through several tool and fidelity paths without granting
  the environment architecture decision authority.

:::

## What Makes a Tool-Connected Environment?

Giving a method permission to run a shell command does not create an
architecture environment. A shell can launch `SIM-A`, but it does not prove
that the `3MB` configuration reached the simulator, that `XR-TRACE-A` was used,
that the cache and power models match the study, or that the expected output
files exist. A zero exit status reports a process outcome. It does not identify
what the process evaluated.

Five terms divide the work:

- A *tool* transforms an artifact or analyzes a stated property under declared
  inputs and conditions. Compilers, SRAM models, simulators, formal engines,
  synthesis tools, and place-and-route flows are tools.
- A *simulator* is one kind of tool. It executes a model of hardware and
  software behavior and returns only the behavior that model exposes. It is not
  the complete environment.
- A *wrapper* surrounds one tool. It validates a request, translates the
  request into tool-specific inputs, invokes the tool, and parses the returned
  files.
- A *harness* coordinates the wrappers and records attempts, state, costs,
  failures, retries, resets, and produced artifacts.
- The *environment* is the complete tool-connected surface available to the
  study. It defines the state a method may observe, the requests it may issue,
  the tools it may reach, and the returns it may receive.

One environment may contain wrappers for an SRAM model, a cycle-level
simulator, a cache model, and a power model. One harness keeps their outputs
tied to the same candidate and conditions.

A usable environment also distinguishes several related terms. *State* is the
full relevant condition of the design, software, tools, runtime, resources,
and outstanding work. An *observation* is the authorized portion of that state,
or a returned result, exposed to the caller. An *action* is a permitted typed
request with identity and preconditions. A *transition* records what changed
when an action was accepted, completed, failed, cancelled, or reset. A tool
*return* is the raw and structured output of one attempt. It is feedback about
that attempt. Later qualification determines whether the return supports an
update, a stopping decision, or no change.

These responsibilities form four parts of an environment. Setup establishes
the starting design, software, workload, tool, and resource state. Interfaces
and wrappers define what may be requested and translate it exactly. The runtime
and harness schedule, isolate, budget, cancel, retry, and record the work.
Finally, the return path preserves execution state, artifacts, parsed results,
warnings, cost, and lineage. The four parts exist whether a learned method, a
conventional search, or an architect issues the request.

The interface has three paths. The read path supplies the represented
candidate, fixed state, tool identities, available resources, and prior
attempts. The action path accepts only declared requests and translates them
exactly. The return path carries execution status, raw artifacts, parsed
fields, unclassified output, cost, and lineage. These paths make the
environment inspectable from both sides (@fig-environment-tool-interface).

![**A tool interface keeps request checking, execution, parsing, and recording
separate.** The wrapper validates and translates one request, while the harness
records the attempt and preserves each return status.](images/F6-environment-tool-interface){#fig-environment-tool-interface fig-alt="An architecture question, action schema, constraints, and metric definitions enter an environment as a typed request. A wrapper separates invalid requests from tool execution. The tool path can fail, return partial output, or complete; the parser retains raw and structured output, and the harness records every outcome with cost, provenance, and execution status."}

The represented question and state enter the interface as a typed request. The
wrapper either refuses an invalid request or translates it to the declared tool
path. That path can fail, return only part of the expected output, or complete,
and the parser keeps the raw output alongside the fields it recognizes. The
harness places every outcome in the record for that attempt with its identity,
cost, provenance, and status. Later work can then distinguish a request that
never ran from a failed, partial, or complete return.

## Why Architecture Environments Are Hard

Architecture environments connect tools that were not designed as one
stateless service. They operate on large, versioned artifacts; preserve hidden
state in working directories and databases; use incompatible formats and
units; wait for shared machines and licenses; and produce partial files after
long failures. A single candidate may require software construction,
simulation, RTL, formal checks, synthesis, and physical implementation. No
generic software sandbox supplies those architecture meanings automatically.

Architecture and electronic design automation (EDA) tools often expose command
shells or text interfaces rather than stateless APIs. OpenROAD and its OpenSTA
timing engine, for example, provide Tcl command interfaces
[@OpenROADDocs]. A wrapper for such a tool must establish or validate
the declared state before each invocation, use the tool's error mechanism to
return an explicit status, and serialize the recognized fields. It must also
retain the raw transcript and any unclassified output. A clean structured
record is useful, but it is not sufficient if an unfamiliar warning was
discarded while the record was built.

Real projects also inherit IP blocks, software, constraints, generated files,
vendor models, and tool databases. The environment need not reveal protected
contents beyond the study's authorization, but it must preserve the exact
identity, version, permitted use, and dependent state carried into each
invocation. Otherwise a repeated request can appear identical while running
against a different design or model.

One legacy SRAM macro, for example, may appear as a behavioral model in
simulation, a Liberty timing and power view during synthesis and timing
analysis, and a LEF physical view during placement and routing. Updating the
behavioral model while retaining an older Liberty or LEF view lets different
tool stages evaluate different versions of what the study treats as one macro.
The environment must bind compatible views to one identity or refuse the run.

Translation must be exact or refused. If the study asks for `l2.capacity=3MB`,
the wrapper may serialize that value into an SRAM configuration file and a
simulator parameter. It may not silently round the value to the nearest
supported capacity, change associativity to make the configuration legal, or
substitute another simulator because it is idle. Each of those choices changes
the meaning of the request. A syntax-preserving repair may create a new request
artifact or execution attempt while retaining the candidate identity. A repair
that changes architecture meaning creates a new candidate and returns to method
selection.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="One cache request, several exact translations"}
The `3MB` candidate becomes one `SRAM-A` input under `PVT-A` and, if the
predeclared routing condition permits, one `SIM-A` configuration linked to
`CACHE-A`, `PM-A`, `XR-TRACE-A`, and `SW-BASE-A`. The wrapper may change file
syntax, paths, and command-line spelling. It may not change cache policy,
associativity, the NoC, compiler, runtime, workload, or another architecture
field. An exact translation proceeds. Anything else is refused and recorded.
:::

This narrow rule prevents a common failure. An automated repair can make a
tool call legal by changing the design that was supposed to be evaluated. The
tool then runs cleanly, but the returned result belongs to a different
candidate. Request validation should catch the mismatch before cluster time is
spent.

## Setup and a Known Starting State

Every requested run begins from a known state. Source and generated artifacts,
workload inputs, tool and library versions, process design kit (PDK) views,
constraints, environment variables, host resources, and baseline artifacts
must be pinned or marked intentionally variable before the first tool starts.
The run specification fixes the relationship among that state, the represented
request, the tool path, and the returned artifacts. It says how the requested
work will run without changing the architecture comparison.

At this point, the run specification must identify the starting state,
permitted translation, tool path, expected returns, budget, and stopping
conditions. Later sections add the failure, retry, reset, containment, and
retention rules needed for a complete environment. The complete Lighthouse
specification appears in @tbl-environment-contract after those responsibilities
have been developed.

### Immutable Inputs, Mutable Work State, and Lineage

Immutable inputs are the versioned source, workload snapshot, constraints,
libraries, PDK views, tool images, and baseline artifacts from which a run
starts. Mutable work state is the run directory, generated files, tool
database, checkpoint, scheduler state, and other state the requested action may
change. The harness never patches the immutable inputs in place. It creates a
new working state linked to them and records every permitted mutation.

Reset means restoring a declared starting state, not merely calling a function
named `reset`. A clean reset regenerates the working directory and tool state
from pinned inputs. A checkpoint reset starts from an identified intermediate
database whose parent inputs and validity conditions still match. Setup checks
must confirm the expected top level, clocks, constraints, libraries, workload,
tool version, and artifact set before scarce execution begins.

Architecture tools rarely consume the representation in which the study was
formulated. An SRAM model reads an organization and technology configuration.
A cycle-level simulator reads a platform description, workload image, and
microarchitecture and platform parameters. A power model may consume activity
and event counts from another tool. The environment lowers one candidate into
these forms while retaining the parent relationship.

Each transformation record names:

- the parent candidate and request;
- the transformation and tool version;
- input identifiers and content hashes where useful;
- fixed conditions inherited from the study;
- the output artifact and its hash;
- whether the transformation may change architecture meaning; and
- the next authorized consumer.

A semantics-preserving serialization keeps the candidate identity. A
semantics-changing edit creates another candidate. This distinction matters
when a wrapper repairs a malformed file. Adding a missing quote around `3MB`
may preserve meaning. Reducing the cache to `2MB` so the parser accepts it does
not.

Content hashes make exact artifacts distinguishable. They do not prove that
two artifacts are functionally equivalent or represent the same architecture.
Build systems such as Bazel illustrate how declared inputs and
content-sensitive action caches can make transformations more inspectable
[@Bazel]. Nondeterministic or undeclared tool state can still defeat
reproducibility, so the harness records the execution conditions as well as the
hash.

Seeds are only one source of variation. Thread counts, scheduler placement,
parallel reduction order, host libraries, timing of concurrent jobs, and
nondeterministic EDA heuristics can change a return even when source inputs
match. The setup should pin these factors where the tool permits. Where it
cannot, the run report states what varied and retains enough repeated attempts
to characterize repeatability later. Controlled nondeterminism is a declared
property of the setup; unrecorded variation is an unknown dependency.

A larger hardware and software change makes the lineage problem visible
(@fig-artifact-lineage). The same root intent may produce several software
binaries and RTL artifacts. Changing one binary while holding the RTL fixed
creates a new evaluation instance even when the root intent has not changed.

![**Every evaluated artifact needs an identifiable parent.** Software and
hardware artifacts derived from one proposal retain their transformation
history, and a changed input creates a new evaluation
identity.](images/F5-artifact-lineage){#fig-artifact-lineage fig-alt="One Lighthouse intent branches into software variant S2 and hardware variant H3. S2 compiles into binary B2, H3 elaborates into RTL R3, and one evaluation instance binds the selected B2 and R3. Identifiers and hashes distinguish exact artifacts and paths but do not prove functional equivalence or reproducibility."}

In the displayed branch, the Lighthouse intent produces software variant `S2`
and hardware variant `H3`. `S2` compiles into binary `B2`, while `H3`
elaborates into RTL `R3`; the selected pair becomes one evaluation instance.
Replacing either child creates a different pair even when the root intent does
not change. The identifiers and hashes distinguish the exact artifacts and
their transformation path. They do not establish functional equivalence or
reproducibility when relevant state remains undeclared.

Conditions need the same discipline. A return retains the conditions that
apply to its tool and marks nonapplicable fields. `SRAM-A` carries circuit and
technology assumptions under `PVT-A`; an implementation return carries its
corner, mode, libraries, constraints, and flags; and `SIM-A`, `CACHE-A`, and
`PM-A` carry workload, software, warm-up, region, seed, checkpoint, and model
configuration. The environment preserves these fields without judging their
sufficiency. A timing-slack return of `-12\ ps` at a slow process corner is not
interchangeable with the same numeric return at a typical corner. The number
travels with the condition that gives it meaning.

The host environment can also change a result. Mytkowicz and colleagues showed
that link order and UNIX environment size can perturb measured performance by
more than many reported optimizations [@Mytkowicz2009WrongData]. An optimizer
with many attempts can exploit such effects. Pinning and recording the binary,
host, environment, and flags prevents an accidental host difference from
masquerading as a candidate difference.

## Interfaces and Wrappers

A wrapper turns the known starting state into one narrow tool interface. Its
request schema names every parameter, type, unit, required input, default, and
legal combination. Its return schema names every structured field, unit,
status, warning class, and raw artifact. A capacity field that means bytes must
not accept an unqualified `3`; a timing result must not omit whether its unit
is cycles, nanoseconds, or simulator ticks.

The interface must also state which project state the caller may read and
which fields it may change. A cache-sizing wrapper can expose capacity while
keeping associativity, policy, interconnect, compiler, runtime, and workload
read-only. The wrapper refuses a request outside that action set. It does not
silently project the request to the nearest supported design. Exact translation
preserves the requested architecture meaning; a meaning-changing repair creates
a new candidate.

Standardization should remove accidental interface differences without hiding
tool meaning. A common core can standardize request identity, permitted
actions, lifecycle status, errors, cost, cancellation, retry, and lineage.
Each wrapper must still expose its supported operations, stages, properties,
fidelities, units, assumptions, defaults, and warnings. This division lets
another method use the harness and another architect interpret its return
without depending on private glue knowledge.

Capability and schema discovery make that division inspectable. Each request
and return records the wrapper, request-schema, return-schema, parser, and tool
versions. A caller can inspect supported actions and fields before submitting
work. An unsupported request is refused rather than silently dropping a field,
changing a default, or substituting another fidelity. A retained request is
never reinterpreted under a newer schema. An explicit migration creates a new
request artifact linked to the original.

Errors are part of the interface. Validation errors, tool diagnostics, missing
outputs, parse failures, and unclassified warnings remain distinct and retain
their original text. A typed result makes routine fields easier to consume, but
the wrapper must not discard output that its current schema does not recognize.
The read, action, and return paths in @fig-environment-tool-interface make
these responsibilities visible.

Structured hardware representations can reduce ambiguity when they match the
artifact. Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT), built on the Multi-Level
Intermediate Representation (MLIR) infrastructure, provides typed operations
for hardware compilation rather than requiring every change to be a textual
source edit [@CIRCT; @LattnerEtAl2020MLIR]. This is one useful interface
mechanism, not the definition of an environment. A shared CIRCT operation,
JSON schema, or simulator request also does not make two tools equal in
fidelity. The tool model, setup, and returned property still determine what
each observation contains.

## Coordinating and Containing Tool Runs

The familiar reinforcement-learning interface calls `step()` and receives an
observation, reward, termination flags, and auxiliary information through a
standard synchronous API [@TowersEtAl2023Gymnasium]. That interface does not
imply that an architecture step is cheap. A cycle simulation may run for hours.
A physical-design job may wait in a queue, hold a scarce license, produce
intermediate databases, and fail after substantial work. Tool state persists
in working directories, caches, checkpoints, license servers, random seeds,
and generated artifacts.

The harness maintains shared state for pending, running, completed, and
cancelled jobs. It attaches each job identifier to the candidate and conditions
at submission rather than when a late result arrives. Dependencies are
explicit. A compiler build may wait for a source artifact, RTL simulation may
wait for elaboration, and physical implementation may wait for a mapped
netlist. Independent jobs may run concurrently, but concurrency does not relax
their identity or resource limits.

Authorization follows least privilege. A wrapper receives only the executables,
filesystem paths, network destinations, credentials, secrets, licensed
features, and intellectual property needed for its declared action. Generated
scripts, constraints, RTL, and compiler inputs are untrusted until validated
and confined. Each attempt uses an isolated working area, resource limits, and
a process boundary. Cancellation must terminate descendants, release licenses,
quarantine uncertain outputs, and preserve enough partial state to explain
what happened.

Budgets apply independently to model calls, tool submissions, elapsed time,
CPU and accelerator use, memory, storage, and license occupancy. Admission
checks reserve scarce resources before dispatch. An accepted request may still
be queued, cancelled, or fail. A completed run may still be missing an
artifact. None of those process states is a valid architecture result by
itself.

Automated work also shares queues, machines, storage, and licenses with
engineers and production flows. The environment applies the site's admission
policy through in-flight limits, project quotas or priorities, reservations,
and backpressure. It exposes pending work, accepted work, and remaining
authorization so a method does not resubmit merely because a queued job is not
yet visible.

The harness therefore needs explicit states rather than one blocking call. A
request is validated and admitted; each authorized attempt is then queued, run,
and brought to a terminal process state. Terminal cause, artifact completeness,
parser status, cancellation status, and retry eligibility are separate fields
rather than additional scheduling states. A process can complete with partial
artifacts, or time out after producing a parseable report. An infrastructure
failure may be retryable, while a cancelled job may not be. None of these
fields says what the candidate means until later measurement qualification.

The execution interface uses two linked records. @lst-environment-interface
keeps the request identifiable from validation through termination.

```{.text #lst-environment-interface lst-cap="**One request remains identifiable through execution:** Request identity, scheduling state, termination, retry, reset, and resource use remain connected."}
envelope, created = create_attempt_once(
    submission_key,
    attempt_id, request_id, candidate_id, condition_id,
    tool_type, tool_stage, fidelity,
    configuration_id, seed, translated_input_hashes,
    retry_parent, reset_parent
)

if not created:
    if immutable request fields differ from the retained attempt:
        refuse reuse of the submission key
    return current_record(envelope.attempt_id)

if translation changes request meaning:
    return envelope(
        terminal_cause=INVALID_REQUEST,
        artifact_status=NOT_CREATED,
        parse_status=NOT_RUN
    )

setup_status = check_setup_and_dependencies(envelope)
if setup_status is not PASSED:
    return envelope(
        terminal_cause=SETUP_FAILURE,
        artifact_status=NOT_CREATED,
        parse_status=NOT_RUN
    )

submission = admit_reserve_and_submit_once(envelope)
if submission.status is REFUSED:
    return envelope(
        terminal_cause=ADMISSION_REFUSED,
        artifact_status=NOT_CREATED,
        parse_status=NOT_RUN
    )

job_id = submission.job_id
record scheduling_state=current_scheduler_state(job_id)

while job is queued or running:
    record scheduling_state, queue_time, and partial_artifact_ids
    if cancellation is authorized:
        request termination
        record cancellation_status=REQUESTED
        break
    if timeout is reached:
        request termination
        record cancellation_status=TIMEOUT_REQUESTED
        break

wait until scheduler and process report a terminal state
if termination cannot be confirmed:
    return open_envelope(
        scheduling_state=UNKNOWN or last_observed_state,
        cancellation_status,
        termination_status=UNCONFIRMED,
        retry_eligibility=NO,
        uncertain_outputs=QUARANTINED
    )
record final scheduler state
record queue_time, run_time, cpu_time, gpu_time,
       peak_memory, storage_written, license_occupancy
```

After the process stops, @lst-environment-return records what happened to the
process, expected artifacts, and parser as separate outcomes.

```{.text #lst-environment-return lst-cap="**The return preserves distinct failure sources:** Process outcome, artifact status, parsing, retry eligibility, cost, and lineage do not collapse into one exit code."}
if terminal state is CANCELLED or TIMED_OUT:
    terminal_cause = CANCELLED or TIMED_OUT
elif setup check fails before or during execution:
    terminal_cause = SETUP_FAILURE
elif process exits:
    record process_outcome, exit_status, run_time, and resource_record
    terminal_cause = COMPLETED or INFRA_FAILURE or TOOL_FAILURE

artifact_status = inspect_expected_artifacts(
    COMPLETE or PARTIAL or MISSING
)

if artifacts can be parsed:
    parse_status = COMPLETE or COMPLETE_WITH_RESIDUAL
    retain typed_fields, unclassified_residual, raw_path, and raw_hash
else:
    parse_status = FAILED or NOT_RUN

return envelope(
    scheduling_state, setup_status, process_outcome, terminal_cause,
    cancellation_status, termination_status,
    artifact_status, parse_status, retry_eligibility,
    resource_record, retry_parent, reset_parent, lineage
)
```

Recording candidate identity before submission prevents late returns from
attaching to whichever candidate is current when a job finishes. Repeating
submission with the same idempotency key returns the existing attempt or job
identifier rather than launching duplicate work. An intentional retry receives
a new attempt identifier, links to its parent, and consumes the declared retry
budget.

Cancellation also remains a request until termination is confirmed. A process
may report cancellation, terminate after producing partial artifacts, or
complete before the cancellation takes effect. The environment retains any
late return under its original attempt. It does not expose that return as a
live observation until the current request revision and budget policy admit
it. The return then separates process completion, expected artifacts, and
parser status so later review can locate the failed work.

The resource record is a typed vector rather than one opaque cost field
(@tbl-attempt-resource-record). Fields that the environment cannot observe
remain explicitly unreported. Human work is linked to the attempt or group of
attempts it supported because setup, diagnosis, and repair can span more than
one invocation.

| **Record group** | **Fields to preserve for each attempt** |
| --- | --- |
| **Tool and work identity** | Tool type, stage, fidelity, version, candidate, conditions, unique configuration, and seed. |
| **Attempt accounting** | Attempt identifier, scheduling state, cancellation status, termination status, terminal cause, artifact completeness, parse status, retry eligibility, retry parent, and reset parent. |
| **Time** | Submission, queue, start, and completion times; queue duration, run duration, and elapsed time. |
| **Compute and storage** | CPU and accelerator time, peak memory where available, intermediate and retained storage, and host or cluster identity when it affects comparability. |
| **Scarce tool resources** | License or token occupancy, reserved capacity, and any admission-control wait. |
| **Model and tool budget** | Model calls, tool submissions, retries, cancellations, and remaining limits for the enclosing request. |
| **Linked human work** | Setup, intervention, diagnosis, review, and repair time, with the responsible activity or role when recorded. |

: **An attempt record preserves resource use and execution status:** Unique
configurations remain separate from invocation attempts, and retries remain
linked rather than increasing apparent sample coverage.
{#tbl-attempt-resource-record tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

The first two rows preserve work identity and attempt accounting. The next four
separate elapsed time, compute and storage, scarce resources, and the enclosing
model and tool budget. The last retains the human work associated with setup,
diagnosis, review, and repair. The decisive distinction is between one unique
configuration and the attempts used to execute it. A retry increases realized
cost but does not create another candidate or another independent observation.

These acquisition conditions must travel with any architecture observation
that later becomes data. Complete-system evaluation can then compare the
resulting resource vectors without treating a cycle simulation, a
physical-design run, and a model call as equivalent samples.

## Failure, Recovery, and Reuse

Retries also need identity. A retry is a new attempt linked to the failed
attempt, not a continuation that erases what happened. The record states which
inputs were reused, which state was reset, which checkpoint was resumed, and
why another attempt was authorized. A scheduler pause that continues the same
submitted job retains its identity; a new job from a checkpoint or a clean
reset creates a linked attempt. Repeated failure under controlled conditions
may expose a reproducible tool problem, but it does not prove physical
infeasibility.

Recovery follows the failure class. Invalid requests are repaired before a
tool runs; setup and parser defects usually require a clean restart after the
wrapper is fixed; and transient host or license failures may permit a retry.
Long implementation runs may resume only from an identified, compatible
checkpoint. If an upgrade caused the failure, reverting to the last pinned
version creates a new attempt rather than rewriting the existing record.

Safe caching follows the same identity rule. A complete return is reusable
only when its inputs, transformations, tools, libraries, PDK views, flags,
conditions, and relevant state all match the cache key. Partial and failed
outputs may support diagnosis, but they are not served as completed
observations. Unknown dependencies invalidate the entry. Reuse saves execution
cost; it does not establish that the retained return answers the present
architecture question.

The 1996 Ariane 5 inquiry documented what happens when a reused component
carries an operating assumption into a changed system [@LionsAriane1996].

::: {.callout-war-story title="Ariane 5 and the reused alignment module"}
**The claim.** Flight-proven inertial-reference software from Ariane 4 was
reused for Ariane 5.

**The gap.** A 64-bit floating-point horizontal-velocity value was converted to
a 16-bit signed integer under a range assumption that held for Ariane 4.
Ariane 5 exceeded that range. The conversion raised an unhandled exception,
and the duplicated inertial systems shut down.

**The lesson.** A previously successful component can fail when its operating
conditions change. An architecture harness must record the version, range,
configuration, and surrounding state assumed by a wrapper or checkpoint, then
recheck those assumptions for the current request.
:::

The lesson is narrower than the accident. Reuse is safe only when the
conditions that made the prior execution meaningful still hold.

Tool isolation protects both the study and shared infrastructure. Each attempt
needs its own filesystem view, process boundary, resource limits, and timeout.
A malformed RTL candidate can otherwise corrupt a shared worktree, fill a
disk, exhaust host memory, or wedge a license process. The harness traps the
failure, retains partial artifacts, and returns control without treating the
candidate as measured.

### Failure Classes and Recovery

Tool paths fail in several ways, and one `FAILED` value cannot represent them.
Terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser status, and retry eligibility
remain separate fields. The rows below show common combinations rather than
one exclusive status value. They determine what the harness repairs and what
it hands forward, so they describe execution rather than architecture judgment
(@tbl-failure-taxonomy).

| **Execution Outcome** | **Example** | **What the Harness Records** | **Next Execution Action** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Invalid request | `l2.capacity=6MB`, missing required workload identity, or a translation that changes associativity. | Refusal reason, request identity, validation rule, and no tool invocation. | Repair syntax under a new request artifact only when meaning is preserved; otherwise create a new candidate and return to method selection. |
| Setup or dependency failure | A stale constraint file, wrong top level, missing clock, corrupt checkpoint, unavailable library, or mismatched generated input reaches the tool path. | Setup identity, expected-state check, returned diagnostics, partial artifacts, and realized cost. | Restore or regenerate the declared state, repair the setup, or revert the affected version. The candidate remains unevaluated. |
| Infrastructure failure | License checkout fails, cluster node dies, shared storage disappears, or a declared host resource is unavailable. | Attempt, failure class, partial artifacts, realized cost, and retry eligibility. | Retry only under the declared policy. The candidate remains unevaluated. |
| Tool failure | A tool crashes, reports an internal error, or exhausts a tool-local resource. The same input may repeat the failure under controlled retries. | Tool status, diagnostics, partial artifacts, realized cost, retry history, and all recorded conditions. | Retry, restart cleanly, resume a valid checkpoint, or stop according to policy. Repetition alone does not prove physical infeasibility. |
| Partial or incomplete return | A tool stops after synthesis but before placement, or exits zero with an expected report absent, stale, or partly written. | Completed and missing stages, expected-artifact check, produced files, raw output, parse status, and terminal cause. | Preserve the partial return; repair or rerun before treating it as complete, and do not convert it automatically into a design score. |
| Parser failure | A retained report does not match the declared schema or contains units, fields, or warnings the parser cannot classify. | Parser version and status, raw report identity, parse diagnostics, recognized fields, and unclassified residual. | Repair or replace the parser and parse the retained raw artifact again when safe. Do not rerun the tool merely to hide a parser defect. |
| Formal solver outcome | A formal engine reports a proof result, counterexample, bounded result, `unknown`, or a resource limit for a named property. | Property, model, assumptions, bound where applicable, solver and version, outcome, counterexample or a proof artifact when the tool emits one, and cost. | Preserve the solver outcome exactly and hand it forward. Do not turn one property result into a general correctness verdict. |
| Reported design-limit violation | A completed timing, power, congestion, design-rule, or functional run reports a declared limit violation. | Typed value or violation, units, candidate and condition identity, warnings, raw artifact, and cost. | Record a complete return and hand it forward without the environment rejecting or penalizing the candidate. |
| Complete tool return | Expected artifacts exist and parse under the declared schema, including reports that contain limit violations. | Typed fields, units, conditions, warnings, raw artifacts, cost, and lineage. | Retain the complete return for measurement qualification without deciding what it establishes. |

: **Execution status determines what ran, not what the architecture means.**
Invalid requests, failed paths, partial returns, parser failures, and complete
returns stay separate so the next repair targets the right problem.
{#tbl-failure-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[18,25,31,26]"}

The retained record and next execution action depend on the observed execution
condition. Invalid requests, setup failures, and infrastructure failures leave
the candidate unevaluated. Tool, artifact, and parser failures identify
different recovery owners. A formal solver outcome and a reported design-limit
violation are completed returns, not process failures, but neither supplies a
broad design verdict. Every completed result goes forward with its scope
intact.

A clean exit becomes a complete tool return only after the expected-artifact
check and parser succeed. Consider a synthesis script that selects no valid
top-level module and omits the primary clock. The process may still exit zero
and produce empty reports. The harness records a completed process together
with missing artifacts and failed setup checks rather than substituting zeros
for area, power, and timing.

Physical-design stages show why a complete return may still contain a reported
limit violation. Synthesis, placement, routing, and signoff expose different
artifacts and limitations (@tbl-eda-stage-interface).

| **Tool Stage** | **Return to Preserve** | **What Is Still Missing** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Logic synthesis | Mapped netlist, area and timing estimates, constraints, warnings, and process status. | Placement, routed interconnect, signoff timing, and power integrity. |
| Floorplanning and placement | Cell and macro locations, utilization, congestion estimates, timing pressure, warnings, and databases. | Routed timing, final design-rule checks, and signoff analysis. |
| Clocking, routing, and power analysis | Routed timing, clock reports, congestion, design-rule results, power estimates, warnings, and databases. | Any property, mode, corner, or system condition outside the declared run. |
| Signoff analysis | Reports tagged with tool, library, corner, mode, constraints, warnings, and waivers. | Architecture interpretation, comparison validity, and authorization to proceed. |

: **Each tool stage returns a different kind of result.** The harness records
the stage and its conditions so an early estimate cannot be mistaken for a
later report.
{#tbl-eda-stage-interface tbl-colwidths="[23,42,35]"}

Each successive stage exposes more implementation artifacts but remains
limited to the modes, corners, and conditions run. Even signoff supplies
neither architecture interpretation nor authorization to proceed.

Raw logs remain part of the return. A commercial EDA tool or a detailed
simulator may emit thousands of lines. Passing all of that text to a model is
impractical, but discarding everything outside a fixed parser is unsafe. The
wrapper should return structured fields for recognized metrics and failures,
an explicitly marked residual of unclassified warnings and errors, and both a
retrievable artifact identifier and integrity hash for the complete raw log.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The parser recognizes only yesterday's warnings"}
**The trap.** A parser keeps only known warning classes and drops every line it
cannot classify.

**The mechanism.** A new warning about a downgraded timing constraint or
changed clock definition appears after a tool upgrade. The parser produces a
clean structured record because it was never taught the new class.

**The lesson.** Preserve unclassified warning and error lines with the raw log.
A compact return should reduce reading cost without granting the parser
permission to decide that unfamiliar output is irrelevant.
:::

The same rule applies to partial returns. A placement density map produced
before a router crash may help later diagnosis, but it remains a partial
artifact. The environment records what stage produced it and what never ran.
Later measurement qualification determines whether that artifact bears on any
claim.

## What Each Run Must Report

A run report joins the requested work to what actually happened. It preserves
both raw output and a structured view, because neither is sufficient alone.
Raw logs, reports, traces, databases, and counterexamples retain details that a
current parser may miss. Structured fields make status, metrics, warnings,
cost, and identity inspectable without rereading every file.

Each report carries seven groups:

- **Identity:** Study, request, candidate, workload, software, conditions,
  parent artifacts, and unique attempt identifiers.
- **Setup:** Source revision, translated input, configuration, tool and model
  versions, libraries, PDK views, modes, corners, constraints, waivers,
  environment variables, host or container, reset parent, and checkpoint.
- **Variation controls:** Seeds, thread counts, scheduler and parallelism
  settings, declared nondeterministic behavior, and repetition index.
- **Status:** Validation, setup, queue, process, cancellation, timeout,
  expected-artifact, parser, and formal-solver outcomes as applicable.
- **Returns:** Raw artifacts and logs, hashes, structured values with units,
  warnings, unclassified residual output, and artifact completeness.
- **Cost:** Model calls, tool calls, queue and run time, compute, memory,
  storage, license occupancy, retries, and linked human work.
- **Lineage:** Parent-child transformations, retry and reset links, cache
  decision, and the next authorized consumer.

The resource fields in @tbl-attempt-resource-record are one part of this
report, not a substitute for the setup and return fields. Unknown or
unobservable values remain explicitly unreported. A missing seed, library
view, or raw report is not repaired by leaving its cell blank.

Three reproducibility claims must remain distinct. *Exact replay* submits the
same retained request, artifacts, versions, and recorded state again. It proves
that the same inputs were requested, not that a nondeterministic tool must
return the same bits. *Repeatability* asks whether repeated runs under the
declared setup agree within the variation that the environment records.
*Independent reproduction* rebuilds the run from the stated specification
without depending on private working state, and may use a separate
implementation or installation. It is stronger operational evidence than
replay, but the returned agreement still must be interpreted against the
property and conditions under study.

Hashes establish the identity and integrity of exact bytes. They do not prove
that two netlists are equivalent, two configurations express the same
architecture, or two runs are semantically comparable. Those relations require
the relevant transformation record and later check.

## Multi-Tool and Multi-Fidelity Environments

Architecture studies often use several tools because no one tool observes
every relevant property. The tools differ in latency, modeled detail, and
returned artifacts. These are not steps on a universal quality scale. An FPGA
emulator may execute a target model much faster than RTL simulation without
providing ASIC placement or timing signoff. A circuit model may estimate SRAM
area and access time without executing the workload.

The useful comparison is what each tool consumes and returns
(@tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum).

| **Tool Class** | **Representative Use** | **What It Models or Checks** | **What the Environment Must Preserve** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical or circuit model | Spreadsheet or CACTI-class SRAM estimate [@MuralimanoharEtAl2009CACTI]. | Encoded equations or circuit and technology assumptions, without workload execution. | Model version, organization, technology assumptions, units, and limits. |
| Compiler and software build | Target compiler, lowering passes, assembler, linker, libraries, and runtime image. | Whether the declared source and mapping produce the expected executable artifacts; no hardware timing or physical result. | Source and intermediate representations, target features, flags, mapping, library and compiler versions, diagnostics, and binary identity. |
| Functional ISA execution | ISA-level functional execution. | Instruction and software behavior under the implemented ISA model, without microarchitectural timing. | Binary, ISA options, input, termination state, and functional output. |
| Cycle-level simulation | gem5-class processor and memory simulation [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5]. | Modeled pipeline, cache, interconnect, and memory timing under a configuration. | Workload, software, warm-up, region, seed, configuration, event counts, and traces. |
| RTL simulation | Verilator-class simulation [@Veripool2026Verilator]. | Cycle behavior under the supplied RTL and simulator semantics; no routed-delay result unless such timing is explicitly supplied. | RTL identity, testbench, compile flags, reset, waves, assertions, and logs. |
| Formal property or equivalence tool | Property checking or equivalence for a named model and relation. | The stated property or equivalence relation within declared assumptions, abstraction, and bound where applicable; no general correctness result. | Property and model identities, assumptions, abstraction, bound, solver version and outcome, proof or counterexample artifact, and cost. |
| FPGA-accelerated emulation | FireSim-class target execution [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. | Accelerated execution of a mapped target model. The FPGA implementation is not ASIC signoff. | Target model, FPGA image, host configuration, workload, and returned traces. |
| Implementation flow | Synthesis, OpenROAD-class place and route, and stage-specific analysis checks [@Yosys; @AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD]. | Properties exposed by the declared stage, libraries, constraints, modes, and corners. | Every intermediate artifact, tool condition, warning, waiver, and stage result. |

: **Tool class constrains the type of return.** The environment retains each
tool's model, inputs, conditions, stage, latency, and artifacts instead of
collapsing several returns into one generic score.
{#tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum tbl-colwidths="[19,22,29,30]"}

A compiler constructs an executable path but does not return hardware timing.
Functional ISA execution returns instruction and software behavior without
microarchitectural timing. Cycle-level and RTL simulation expose different
timing and logic behavior, while a formal tool reports only the property and
model it received. FPGA execution does not establish ASIC implementation
results. An implementation flow remains limited to its declared stages,
libraries, constraints, modes, and corners. The tool class therefore
determines the type of return, not a universal quality rank.

For one prospective `L2-3M-A` environment, each row names a distinct branch
from the same candidate. `SRAM-A` receives the exact cache organization and
`PVT-A`. The compiler branch binds `SW-BASE-A`, target features, libraries,
flags, and runtime to a hashed binary. The cycle-level branch binds that binary
and candidate to `XR-TRACE-A`, `SIM-A`, `CACHE-A`, `PM-A`, warm-up, seed, and
checkpoint. RTL simulation adds generated RTL, a testbench, compile flags, and
reset. Formal checking adds one named property or equivalence relation,
assumptions, abstraction, bound, and solver. Logic synthesis adds top-level
constraints and libraries; physical implementation adds floorplan, PDK views,
modes, corners, and waivers.

The branches are not interchangeable. The compiler reports an executable path,
not hardware timing; the simulator reports only modeled workload behavior; RTL
simulation has no routed delay unless explicitly annotated; and formal results
cover only the submitted property and model. Synthesis is not a routed
implementation, while physical results remain scoped to completed stages,
views, modes, corners, and waivers. Only the SRAM and cycle-level branches
belong to the constructed trace below. The environment preserves every
branch's input, raw and structured return, cost, and limit without promoting or
rejecting `L2-3M-A`.

Throughput changes how many candidates and conditions a study can afford to
examine. In one published configuration, ZSim ran a detailed Westmere-class
out-of-order model at 20 million simulated instructions per second, about
$200\times$ slower than the modeled core. The same study reported conventional
detailed simulators at roughly 100 to 200 thousand simulated instructions per
second [@ZSim]. FireSim reports a different regime. Individual
FPGA-accelerated target nodes can run at tens to hundreds of megahertz, while
one 1,024-node configuration ran at 3.4\ MHz for 3.2\ GHz targets, a slowdown
of less than $1{,}000\times$ [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim].

Those rates are examples, not constants for a tool class. The modeled system,
host or FPGA allocation, workload, instrumentation, accuracy, and simulation
scale all change the rate. The environment should therefore record the
observed throughput and its conditions, and a method should budget evaluations
from that scoped rate rather than from a generic label such as *cycle-level* or
*FPGA-accelerated*.

Sampling and checkpoint policy are part of that identity. SimPoint selects
representative program regions, while SMARTS supplies a statistical basis for
sampled simulation [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint; @WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. The
environment records the chosen regions, weights, warm-up, fast-forward policy,
and checkpoint parent. It does not decide whether those choices support the
intended comparison.

ArchGym shows the value of exposing several architecture simulators through a
shared interface under controlled budgets [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. Real
project environments need additional state. Jobs wait in queues, hold licenses,
resume checkpoints, and return at different times. A common interface should
make those differences visible rather than hide them behind one `step()` call.

Chipyard provides a concrete multi-tool example. Its Chisel generators and
FIRRTL compiler, built around a hardware intermediate representation, can turn
one configuration into RTL for simulation, VLSI implementation flows, and
FPGA emulation [@chipyard]. The fan-out is useful because every branch retains
the configuration that created it (@fig-chipyard-framework).

![**One configuration can feed several authorized tool paths.** Chipyard
generates related artifacts for RTL simulation, VLSI work, and FPGA emulation
while retaining a common configuration
source.](images/F6b-chipyard-framework){#fig-chipyard-framework fig-alt="A flow diagram of the Chipyard framework. A configuration system feeds Chisel generators and the FIRRTL compiler, then fans out to RTL simulation, a VLSI flow, and FPGA emulation."}

The common configuration passes through the Chisel generators and FIRRTL
compiler before it fans out to RTL simulation, the VLSI flow, and FPGA
emulation. It preserves a shared parent for the three branches, but each branch
produces a different artifact and examines different properties. The fan-out
does not imply a fixed execution order or make the branch results
interchangeable.

The environment may execute independent branches in parallel and dependent
branches in order. Workflow systems such as Nextflow and Snakemake show how a
dependency graph can separate workflow logic from execution on local machines
or computing clusters [@DiTommasoEtAl2017Nextflow;
@KosterEtAl2012Snakemake]. The run specification remains in charge. The
scheduler may plan authorized work, but it may not add a tool, skip a required
branch, or change fidelity without a new request.

Applicable inexpensive prerequisite checks should run before expensive
dependent work. If a declared syntax, interface, functional, or equivalence
check reports that an artifact failed a predeclared prerequisite, the harness
records the return and suppresses only the dependent dispatch before synthesis
or physical implementation. It does not issue an architecture verdict. This is
not one universal tool order. The requested run determines the prerequisites
for each branch, and later measurement qualification determines what a passing
or failing check establishes.

For `XR-L2-CAP-A`, the graph stays small. Three independent `SRAM-A` calls
precede the cycle-level branch. The shared 2\ MB baseline and each eligible
alternative use the same `SIM-A`, `CACHE-A`, `PM-A`, workload, software, and
condition identities. An authorized retry creates a retry edge. It does not
create another candidate.

The complete run specification can now collect the responsibilities developed
throughout the chapter in one place (@tbl-environment-contract).

| **Run Field** | **`XR-L2-CAP-A` Run Specification** |
| --- | --- |
| **Study and request identity** | Study `XR-L2-CAP-A`, request definition `CONTRACT-A`, design revision `XR-COMPUTE-A`, and the selected approach. |
| **Candidates and fixed state** | `L2-2M-A`, `L2-3M-A`, and `L2-4M-A`; cache policy `CACHE-POLICY-A`; NoC `NOC-A`; memory system `MEMSYS-A`; compiler `COMPILER-A`; runtime `RUNTIME-A`; software image `SW-BASE-A`; and workload snapshot `XR-TRACE-A` with stable frame identifiers. |
| **Permitted translation** | Serialize only `l2.capacity` values `2MB`, `3MB`, and `4MB` into declared `SRAM-A` and `SIM-A` inputs. A wrapper may change syntax and file layout but may not change architecture meaning. |
| **Tool and condition identities** | `SRAM-A` under `PVT-A`, followed by `SIM-A` with `CACHE-A` and `PM-A`. The record retains exact versions or hashes, relevant flags, host or container identity, seeds, and reset state. |
| **Execution order** | Run one SRAM evaluation per capacity. After the required area and access-time fields parse successfully, dispatch no `SIM-A` attempt for a capacity whose returned area exceeds `1.5\ mm^2^` or whose returned access time exceeds `2.5\ ns`. This predeclared predicate controls only the next tool call and does not label the candidate rejected. Run the shared 2\ MB baseline and other authorized alternatives under matched workload and software conditions. |
| **Expected returns** | Area, access time, cache-local energy and leakage, matched frame records, 99th-percentile frame-time inputs, capacity misses, subsystem dynamic and leakage power, warnings, reports, and raw logs. |
| **Budget and stop** | Three SRAM evaluations and no more than four cycle-level attempts, including infrastructure reruns. Stop on budget exhaustion, missing required inputs or tools, no eligible alternative, or completion of all authorized work. |
| **Failure and retry behavior** | Refuse invalid requests before invocation. Record timeouts, cancellations, license failures, host failures, stale-state failures, missing outputs, and parser failures separately. A retry creates a new attempt linked to its parent and consumes the declared run budget. |
| **Reset, checkpoint, and cache behavior** | Build each SRAM input from the represented candidate. Start every clean `SIM-A` attempt in a new work directory generated from `XR-COMPUTE-A` and the fixed condition set. A retry regenerates that state rather than resuming the stale directory. The initial live history is empty, so no cached evaluation return may be reused. A generated build artifact may be reused only when the complete declared build action matches, including inputs, transformation and tool versions, flags, conditions, and relevant environment state. |
| **Permissions and containment** | Allow only the declared executables, filesystem paths, network access, credentials, and resource limits. Treat generated scripts and RTL as untrusted inputs until their permitted actions are checked. Define interruption, revocation, quarantine, clean-state restoration, and which partial artifacts survive containment. |
| **Artifact retention** | Retain translated inputs, commands, standard output and error, reports, matched frame records, parsed fields, unclassified warnings, output hashes, and parent-child lineage. |
| **What the environment may not decide** | Whether a return is a valid measurement, whether two returns form a valid comparison, whether a physical limit establishes rejection, or whether a candidate should advance. |

: **A run specification prevents tool mechanics from rewriting the study.**
The request, translation, state, expected outputs, failure behavior, cost, and
limits are fixed before invocation.
{#tbl-environment-contract tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

The upper rows preserve the identities and fixed state through translation.
The middle rows bind those identities to the tool order, expected returns,
budget, and stopping conditions. The execution-order row is the hinge. Its
SRAM predicate may suppress a later simulator call, but it does not reject the
candidate. The lower rows define failure, retry, reset, permissions,
containment, retention, and the decisions the environment cannot make.

This specification must still be written before the first tool call. Filled
afterward, it cannot refuse a bad translation or require a missing output. It
may authorize host selection, license reservation, pause, and resume, but
substituting a tool path, serving stale state, or skipping the baseline requires
a new request.

### The Lighthouse Run Report

To make run reporting concrete, this chapter introduces a constructed trace for
the prospective cache study. It is an author-created teaching example, not live
project history or measurements from tools run for this book. It contains
illustrative SRAM, power, and miss returns, one stale-state failure, and a
four-attempt cycle-level chronology. The table carries the exact values and
their record status. They exercise the record rather than predict the
Lighthouse design, and fields absent from the construction remain marked
unreported.

| **Constructed Attempt** | **Candidate and Constructed State** | **Constructed Outcome and Record Status** | **Return Included in the Teaching Trace** | **Known Cost and Lineage** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `SRAM-2-A1` | `L2-2M-A` under `PVT-A`; the exact serialized input is unreported. | Constructed execution included; record intentionally incomplete. | Area `1.2\ mm^2^` and access time `2.1\ ns`. Cache-local energy and leakage, raw report identity, and parse status are unreported. | One SRAM call; child candidate is known; all other cost and lineage fields are unreported. |
| `SRAM-3-A1` | `L2-3M-A` under `PVT-A`; the exact serialized input is unreported. | Constructed execution included; record intentionally incomplete. | Area `1.4\ mm^2^` and access time `2.4\ ns`. Cache-local energy and leakage, raw report identity, and parse status are unreported. | One SRAM call; child candidate is known; all other cost and lineage fields are unreported. |
| `SRAM-4-A1` | `L2-4M-A` under `PVT-A`; the exact serialized input is unreported. | Constructed execution included; record intentionally incomplete. | Area `1.7\ mm^2^` and access time `2.8\ ns`. Cache-local energy and leakage, raw report identity, and parse status are unreported. | One SRAM call. The trace includes no `SIM-A` request and places area and access time above the dispatch limits. Parser status and the exact dispatch event remain unreported. This is a constructed scheduling outcome, not a design verdict. |
| `SIM-2-A1` | `L2-2M-A`, `XR-TRACE-A`, and `SW-BASE-A`; exact clean-state identity unreported. | Constructed clean execution included; record intentionally incomplete. | Matched baseline frame data and subsystem dynamic plus leakage power `2.90\ W` are included. Attempt-level artifact and parser fields are unreported. | Cycle attempt 1 of 4; baseline relationship known; other cost and lineage fields unreported. |
| `SIM-3-A1` | `L2-3M-A` with stale constraint state. | The trace includes a stale-state setup failure. | No candidate return. Diagnostic and partial-artifact identities are unreported. | Cycle attempt 2 of 4. A later clean attempt is included, but retry parent, reset mechanism, and reset-state identity are unreported. |
| `SIM-3-A2` | `L2-3M-A`; one of two clean attempts under conditions constructed as matched to baseline. | Constructed clean execution included; attempt-level completeness unverified. | Aggregate frame, cache, and power results span both clean 3\ MB attempts rather than this attempt alone. | Cycle attempt 3 of 4; exact parent, cost, and output lineage unreported. |
| `SIM-3-A3` | `L2-3M-A`; the clean repeatability attempt under conditions constructed as matched to baseline. | Constructed clean execution included; attempt-level completeness unverified. | Aggregate frame, cache, and power results span both clean 3\ MB attempts rather than this attempt alone. | Cycle attempt 4 of 4; budget exhausted; exact parent, cost, and output lineage unreported. |

: **An execution record preserves missing information as carefully as returned
values.** The constructed cache chronology retains candidate state, failure,
successor attempts, and call counts without claiming real measurements,
attempt-level provenance, or completeness.
{#tbl-lighthouse-execution-record tbl-colwidths="[12,19,19,25,25]"}

The SRAM rows establish the first three calls, and the simulator rows carry the
four-attempt chronology. The 4\ MB row records no simulator request, the stale
3\ MB attempt returns no candidate result, and the two later clean attempts
share aggregate values without attempt-level attribution. The table therefore
supports a teaching chronology and budget account, not a complete measurement
record or candidate decision.

The trace includes three aggregate values across the clean 3\ MB returns.
Capacity misses fall `12%` relative to baseline, cache leakage rises `2\ mW`,
and modeled subsystem dynamic plus leakage power rises from `2.90\ W` to
`2.94\ W`. The teaching scenario also declares that matched frame sequences
were used to produce an illustrative `0.3\ ms` tail-latency reduction with a
95 percent interval from `-0.1\ ms` to `0.7\ ms`. The record does not retain
those sequences or their identifiers. It also does not assign the aggregate
values to one clean attempt or identify which tool supplied the cache-leakage
difference. The constructed record therefore binds them to the two-attempt
clean-return set rather than to `SIM-3-A2`, `SIM-3-A3`, or `SRAM-3-A1`
individually.

The missing fields extend beyond cost. Exact translated-input hashes, tool and
model versions, host or container identity, seeds, job identifiers and
timestamps, parser status, expected-artifact checks, raw artifact identifiers
and hashes, frame identifiers, checkpoint identity, and the reset action are
all unreported. Wall-clock, queue, license, storage, and other resource costs
are also unreported. These absences make the constructed record incomplete
under @tbl-environment-contract.

The trace supplies three SRAM calls, four cycle-level attempts, one stale-state
setup failure, two later clean 3\ MB attempts, and total call-budget
consumption. It does not supply the complete execution record defined in
@sec-architecture-20-ontology. A production harness would capture the missing
fields at submission and completion rather than ask an architect to reconstruct
them later.

The record includes but cannot recompute the illustrative paired
block-resampling interval. It does not label the 4\ MB candidate invalid, call
the 3\ MB result unresolved, or recommend an architecture action. Those
statements require measurement qualification and comparison.

## Open Research Questions

The open problems concern how environments can preserve requested meaning,
control real tool state, and expose enough evidence about each run without
assuming authority over architecture decisions.

### Interfaces That Preserve Meaning

**How can a wrapper establish that a tool-specific input preserves the requested
architecture change?** Syntax and schema checks catch malformed inputs, but
semantic drift can occur through defaults, rounding, generated collateral, or
unsupported combinations.

**How should a shared interface expose differences in model fidelity and
unknown output?** A common schema can simplify orchestration while hiding
different tool assumptions or discarding warnings its parser does not know.

### Stateful and Protected Tool Use

**What reset is sufficient for a stateful architecture tool?** Working
directories, databases, caches, random seeds, license state, and host state can
survive different kinds of restart.

**What is the smallest useful authority for generated tool inputs?** Build
scripts, RTL, constraints, and tool commands may require selected files,
licenses, and executables without needing unrestricted credentials, network
access, or shared-directory mutation.

**How can a late tool return remain semantically valid after the surrounding
study changes?** Long jobs may complete after the study has issued newer
requests, changed a checkpoint, or exhausted its budget. Correct identity is
necessary but does not establish that the result still answers the live
question.

### Reproducible Multi-Tool Runs

**How can a cache key expose hidden tool dependencies that determine whether
an architecture result remains reusable?** Candidate, software, workload,
tool, model, condition, and freshness can all change the return, while an
opaque tool may not reveal which dependencies its cache actually captures.

**How can independent reproduction survive unavailable tool versions and
proprietary views?** Exact byte identity may be impossible outside the original
site even when another environment can reproduce the declared transformation
or check.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="A trustworthy run makes its state and limits visible"}
Start from pinned inputs, grant only the authority the requested tools need,
and retain the raw and structured return from every attempt. A wrapper may
translate syntax, and a harness may schedule, isolate, retry, reset, or resume
work. Neither may silently change the candidate, conditions, tool path, or
requested meaning.
:::

A tool-connected environment defines state, legal actions, observations,
transitions, costs, stopping conditions, and failure behavior around its tools.
Its wrappers validate and translate typed requests. Its harness manages mutable
state, dependencies, queues, retries, resets, containment, resources, and
lineage under the run specification.

Each attempt reports candidate, workload, conditions, constraints, waivers,
versions, seeds, status, warnings, metrics, artifacts, and realized cost.
Invalid requests, setup, infrastructure, tool, and parser failures, incomplete
artifacts, formal outcomes, and measured violations remain distinct. So do
exact replay, repeatability, and independent reproduction; hashes establish
byte identity rather than semantic equivalence.

The Lighthouse teaching trace carries the constructed cache candidates and
conditions through the named `SRAM-A`, `SIM-A`, `CACHE-A`, and `PM-A` path. It
includes the stale-state setup failure, later clean attempts, illustrative
returns, and consumed call budget. It also identifies the reset mechanism,
exact artifacts, tool conditions, and realized resource costs as missing.
Nothing is filled in simply because a complete-looking record would be easier
to read.

The prospective multi-tool path shows how that same candidate identity could
feed a compiler, simulator, RTL simulation, formal check, synthesis, and
physical implementation while every branch retains its own setup and limits.
The environment reports what each branch did; it does not collapse the returns
into a score, promote a candidate, or decide whether a claim is valid.

The illustrative return values, call counts, setup failure, aggregate
clean-return group, and explicit missing fields are therefore inputs to later
measurement qualification. They do not yet establish which fields are valid
measurements, which comparisons are sound, what the checks can see, or what
the result supports. Measurement qualification is the next task, developed in
@sec-feedback-verification-trust. It determines how the returned measurements
can become useful feedback.
